excerpt: Working through a laptop that will not wake: the power checks first, the external monitor test, and the point where the machine needs a repair shop.

body.text: This lesson is for the moment a laptop screen stays black. You will work through the simple causes first, test whether the machine is running at all, and know when to stop and take it to a repair shop.
A dark screen is not the same as a dead laptop. In many cases the machine is running, the screen is not showing anything, and the difference decides what to do next.
Before you start

items: The laptop and its charger.
A torch or the phone's light.
Ten minutes, and no rush.

body.text: Power first, always

items: Plug the charger in and look for a light on the laptop or the charger.
Leave it for twenty minutes, since a completely flat battery shows nothing at all.
Check the socket with another device, such as a phone charger.
Press the power button once and wait ten seconds.
Then hold it for ten seconds to force a restart.
Listen for the fan or the drive, which tells you the machine is alive.

body.text: You will see the charger light come on if power is reaching the laptop, and that single light rules out the battery and the cable. If it stays dark, the problem is power rather than the screen.

body.alt: A torch shining on a dark laptop screen to check for a faint image.
body.caption: Shine a torch at an angle. A faint image means the screen's backlight has failed, and the machine itself is working.

body.text: It looks like a black screen means the laptop is finished. A backlight, a loose cable, or a stuck sleep state produces the same black rectangle, and all three are repairable.
Is it running?
Before touching anything else, find out whether the computer is alive. Two tests answer that in a minute.

items: Shine a torch across the screen at an angle and look for a faint desktop.
Press the caps lock key and watch for its small light.
Plug in a mouse and see whether its light comes on.
Listen for the fan spinning up when you press power.
Try the brightness key combination, which is often a function key with a sun symbol.
If nothing responds, hold the power button until it switches off completely, then start again.

body.text: A faint image under the torch means the screen works and its light does not. That is a cheaper repair than a dead machine, and worth saying clearly at the shop.

body.alt: A laptop connected to an external monitor by an HDMI cable.
body.caption: An external monitor answers the question in one cable. A picture there means the laptop runs and the screen does not.

body.text: The external screen test

items: Connect any monitor or television with an HDMI cable.
Switch the television to the right input, which is the step people miss.
Press the key that sends the picture to the external screen, usually with two rectangles.
Wait fifteen seconds for the display to wake.
If a picture appears, the laptop is fine and the screen or its cable is the fault.
If nothing appears on either screen, the fault is deeper and needs a shop.

body.text: None of this needs a technician. A cable, a television, and one key combination settle the question in two minutes.
Do not worry about pressing the wrong keys. Nothing on the keyboard can damage the machine, and the display key can always be pressed again.
Memory, if you are confident
On an older laptop with a removable memory stick, reseating it fixes a surprising number of black-screen starts. Stop here if the machine is under warranty.

items: Switch off and unplug the charger.
Remove the battery if it comes out with a latch.
Open the small panel on the underside with a screwdriver.
Press the two clips outward and lift the memory stick out.
Wipe the gold contacts with a clean pencil eraser, then blow away the dust.
Seat it firmly until both clips click, then reassemble and start.

body.alt: A memory stick held by its edges with the gold contacts visible.
body.caption: Hold the stick by the edges and clean the gold contacts gently. A reseated stick fixes a start that stops before the screen.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here has a next step, and stopping early is part of the lesson.

items: The charger light stays off: try another charger of the same rating before opening anything.
The fan spins but nothing shows: use the torch test and the external monitor test.
The laptop beeps in a pattern: that pattern names the faulty part, and a shop will read it.
It starts, then blacks out: the battery or the power circuit needs a technician.
You cannot open the case: stop, since forcing a clip breaks the shell.
The machine is under warranty: take it in, because opening it usually ends the warranty.

body.text: Practice
Rehearse the first three checks before you ever need them.

items: Find the charger light on your laptop.
Note the key combination that switches displays.
Find the brightness keys by touch.
Check whether the battery comes out with a latch.
Write the shop's number in your contacts.

body.text: You can now tell a dark screen from a dead machine. In the next lesson you will deal with a laptop that is overheating before it damages itself.

excerpt: Why a laptop fan gets loud, the dust that causes most of it, and the cooling habits that prevent a machine cooking itself.

body.text: This lesson is about a laptop that runs hot and noisy. You will find the cause, clear the dust that produces most of it, and change the habits that keep a machine cool. Overheating shortens a laptop's life and slows it down long before it fails.
A fan spins faster when the inside is hot. That noise is the machine asking for help, and dust is the usual reason it cannot breathe.
Before you start

items: The laptop, and a place with good light.
A soft brush or a clean paintbrush.
A can of compressed air if you can get one, or a hair dryer on cool.
About thirty minutes.

body.text: Find the heat

items: Feel the underside after ten minutes of work, away from the vents.
Notice where the warm air leaves the machine, usually at the back or the side.
Check whether the vents are blocked by a cushion, a bed, or a cloth.
Listen for the fan starting the moment you open a browser.
Watch whether the noise follows one program, such as a video call.
Note the room temperature, since a hot afternoon changes everything.

body.text: You will see dust gathered along the vent grille, often as a grey mat. That mat is the reason the fan runs at full speed on a task it used to handle silently.

body.alt: A laptop heatsink with a thick layer of dust across the fins.
body.caption: Dust forms a mat across the fins. Air cannot pass through a mat, and the fan cannot cool what the air cannot reach.

body.text: It looks like the fan is failing because it has become loud. The fan is working harder because the path is blocked, and cleaning costs nothing.
Clear the path

items: Switch off and unplug the laptop, and let it cool for ten minutes.
Hold a vent with the brush and loosen the dust along the grille.
Blow short bursts of air into the vent, keeping the fan from spinning fast.
Do not use a vacuum cleaner close to the board, which can loosen small parts.
Clean the vents once a month in a dusty room, twice a year otherwise.
Never open the case if the machine is under warranty.

body.text: The vents will look clear afterwards, with air moving easily when you blow across them. If the noise does not change, the machine needs a professional clean, which includes new thermal paste.
A program's window will show the processor load as a percentage, and a figure near a hundred while nothing is open is the clue. Close that program and the fan drops within a minute.

body.alt: A laptop raised on a wooden stand so air can pass underneath.
body.caption: Raise the back of the machine so air passes underneath. A stand made from wood costs nothing and fixes half the problem.

body.text: Habits that keep it cool

items: Work on a hard surface, never on a bed or a cushion.
Raise the back edge with a stand, a book, or a block of wood.
Keep the laptop out of direct sun, and away from a hot wall.
Close the programs you are not using, since each one adds heat.
Avoid charging and working hard at the same time where you can.
Take a break in a long video call, which is the heaviest ordinary task.

body.text: None of this needs a cooling pad with lights. A wooden stand and a clear vent do more than most accessories sold for the purpose.
Do not worry about the fan running during a call. Some noise is normal, and the machine is designed to manage it.
Thermal paste, and when to stop
Repasting means replacing the grey compound between the processor and its metal plate. It helps a machine over five years old, and it is not a first step.

items: Try cleaning and raising the machine first, which fixes most cases.
If it still overheats, a shop can repaste it in an hour.
The paste is applied as a small dot, not a thick layer.
Ask for the old paste to be cleaned off properly before the new one.
Check that the fan spins freely before the case is closed.
Keep the receipt, since a bad repaste shows within a week.

body.alt: A small dot of thermal paste on a processor before the heatsink is fitted.
body.caption: A dot the size of a grain of rice, spread by the pressure of the heatsink. More paste does not mean better cooling.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here is a normal laptop problem, and each has a sensible next step.

items: The machine shuts down suddenly: it is protecting itself. Stop working and clean the vents.
The fan screams from the moment it starts: something is running, so check the program list.
The underside is hot enough to sting: stop using it on a soft surface today.
The fan rattles: a bearing is failing, and a replacement fan is a cheap repair.
The laptop is under warranty: take it in before opening anything.
Cleaning did not help: ask the shop to check the paste and the fan together.

body.text: Practice
Clean one vent this week, and change one habit.

items: Switch off and let the machine cool.
Brush the vent grille and blow short bursts of air.
Raise the back edge with a book or a stand.
Note the noise before and after.
Write the date of the next clean in your notebook.

body.text: You can now keep a laptop cool enough to last. In the next lesson you will read the sounds a failing drive makes.

excerpt: Recognising a failing hard drive, backing up before it dies, and what a solid-state upgrade does for an older laptop.

body.text: This lesson is about a hard drive that is failing: the sounds, the slowdowns, and the backup you must take today. You will also learn what a solid-state drive changes, and when an upgrade is worth the money.
A mechanical hard drive stores data on spinning plates. When it begins to fail, it clicks, slows, and eventually stops, and the data goes with it unless a copy exists elsewhere.
Before you start

items: The laptop in question, switched on.
A memory stick or an external drive with enough space.
About an hour, and a calm approach.

body.text: The signs

items: A repeating click or tick, especially when a file opens.
Long pauses when saving, with the machine apparently frozen.
Files that disappear, or open with an error about being corrupt.
A startup that takes minutes where it used to take seconds.
A grinding sound that changes as the machine works.
A warning message from the drive's own health check.

body.text: You will see the clicking repeat in time with the work the machine is doing, rather than steadily. That pattern is the drive struggling to read, which is the moment to copy files rather than to run repairs.

body.alt: A drive health window showing a warning status and a reallocated sector count.
body.caption: A health check that reads caution is a warning rather than a diagnosis. Copy the files first, and read the details afterwards.

body.text: It looks like the drive can be repaired with software. A mechanical fault cannot be fixed by a program, and every hour of use shortens the time you have to copy the data.
Back up before anything else
Copy the most important files first, in order of what you could not replace. Everything else waits.

items: Start with documents, then photographs, then everything else.
Copy in small batches, since one bad folder can fail a whole transfer.
Do not run a repair or a defragment on a clicking drive.
Keep the machine cool and still while copying.
Check that each batch opens on the new device before deleting anything.
Stop using the laptop for work until the copy is complete.

body.text: The copy will be slower than usual, and some files will fail with an error. Note which ones failed, and try those again one at a time.

body.alt: A drive connected to a laptop by a USB adapter cable.
body.caption: A drive removed and connected by a USB adapter can be copied from another machine when the laptop will not start.

body.text: The solid-state cure
A solid-state drive has no moving parts, so it is faster and quieter, and it makes an old laptop feel new.

items: Check that the laptop takes a 2.5 inch drive or an M.2 stick before buying.
A 250 or 500 gigabyte drive is enough for ordinary work.
Ask the shop to clone the old drive if it still reads, which avoids reinstalling.
Otherwise install the system fresh, then copy your files back.
Keep the old drive for a month, in case a file was missed.
Expect the machine to start in seconds rather than minutes.

body.text: None of this needs a new laptop. An upgrade of the drive and a clean of the fan restores most five-year-old machines to useful work.
Do not worry about reinstalling being complicated. The shop does it in an hour, and your files are on the old drive throughout.

body.alt: An older laptop opened with a new solid-state drive beside the old one.
body.caption: Old drive out, new drive in. The machine starts faster, and the old drive stays as a backup for a month.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here has a next step, and the first one is about stopping the damage.

items: The drive clicks and the machine will not start: stop trying, and take it to a recovery service.
A folder will not copy: copy the files inside it one by one, and skip what fails.
The new drive is not recognised: it needs formatting, which the shop can do.
The clone fails: install the system fresh and copy the files across.
The laptop is under warranty: ask before opening, since the warranty may cover the drive.
You deleted a file by mistake: check the recycle bin before doing anything else.

body.text: Practice
Run a health check this week, whatever your machine is doing.

items: Look for the drive check tool in the system settings.
Note the health status and the number of hours used.
Copy one important folder to a memory stick.
Open three files from the copy to check they work.
Write down what a replacement drive would cost.

body.text: You can now hear a failing drive in time. In the next lesson you will deal with a spill before it ruins the board.

excerpt: The first ten minutes after a spill: switch off, unplug, turn it upside down, and the drying that must not involve a hair dryer.

body.text: This lesson is for the moment a drink goes over a laptop. You will learn the first ten minutes, which decide whether the machine survives, and the drying rules that stop a small spill becoming a dead board.
Liquid and electricity do not mix, and the damage is caused by power flowing while the board is wet. Cutting the power immediately is the single most useful action.
Before you start

items: The laptop, and whatever spilled.
A dry towel and a flat surface.
Ten minutes of speed, and no shaking.

body.text: The first ten minutes

items: Switch the machine off at once, holding the power button if needed.
Unplug the charger from the wall and from the laptop.
Remove any external drives and memory sticks.
Tip the machine into a tent shape, keyboard face down, so liquid runs out.
Blot the surface with a dry towel, without pressing liquid into the keys.
Leave it in that position for at least twenty-four hours.

body.text: You will see liquid run out of the keys when it is tipped, which is what you want. Every drop that leaves the machine is a drop that is not reaching the board.

body.alt: A hand pulling a charger from a laptop in a hurry.
body.caption: The charger comes out first, then the power button. Power flowing through a wet board is what causes the damage.

body.text: It looks like drying it with heat is faster. Heat warps the case and pushes moisture deeper, and a hair dryer is the worst tool in the house for this job.
The tent position

items: Open the lid and stand the machine on its edges, like a roof.
Put a towel underneath to catch what runs out.
Keep it away from a fan or a heater, which blow dust and heat inward.
Do not press the keys, which pushes liquid further in.
Do not plug it in to test it after an hour.
Wait a full day, and longer if the spill was sugary or milky.

body.text: The towel will show a damp patch after a few hours, which tells you the drying is working. Water takes a day, and sweet drinks take longer because they leave a sticky residue.

The screen will stay black until the machine is properly dry, and that is the correct behaviour rather than a bad sign. Wait the full day before pressing the power button, because the first test is the one that decides.

body.alt: A laptop standing on its edge in a tent shape with a towel beneath it.
body.caption: The tent position lets gravity do the work. Wait a full day, and do not test it early.

body.text: Sugar, tea, and milk
Sweet liquids are worse than water, because the residue conducts and corrodes after the water has gone.

items: Do not switch it on, even if it looks dry after a day.
Take it to a repair shop and say exactly what spilled.
Ask for the board to be cleaned with isopropyl alcohol.
Expect to pay for the cleaning, which is cheaper than a new board.
Keep the storage drive, which usually survives and holds your files.
Do not attempt the cleaning yourself unless you have done it before.

body.text: None of this guarantees recovery. It does improve the odds, and the odds are worth much more than the ten minutes of calm it takes.
Do not worry about having done it. Almost every laptop user has spilled something, and the repair shop sees it weekly.

body.alt: A circuit board being cleaned with isopropyl alcohol and a soft brush.
body.caption: A board cleaned with isopropyl alcohol after a sugary spill. The residue, not the water, is what corrodes the contacts.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here has a next step, and honesty at the shop helps most.

items: It starts and then fails: switch off, and take it in for cleaning before using it again.
The keys stick: the residue needs cleaning, which is a shop job.
It will not charge: the charging circuit is affected, and that is a board repair.
You plugged it in too early: say so at the shop, since it changes the diagnosis.
The shop says the board is dead: ask them to recover the drive.
It works and then behaves oddly: back up immediately, since the damage may spread.

body.text: Practice
Rehearse the first three steps mentally, once.

items: Find where the charger connects.
Practise holding the power button for ten seconds.
Clear a place where the laptop could stand on its edge.
Keep a dry towel within reach of the desk.
Decide now that drinks go on the floor, not beside the keyboard.

body.text: You can now give a wet laptop its best chance. In the next lesson you will buy a used machine without being cheated.

excerpt: Checking a used laptop before you pay: the battery report, the keyboard test, the hinge, and the questions a seller must answer.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to buy a used laptop without being cheated. You will run three quick tests, inspect the parts that fail first, and ask questions a seller cannot dodge. It takes twenty minutes and saves a month of regret.
A used laptop is a good buy when the machine is sound and a bad buy when the battery, the hinge, or the drive is failing. Each of those is testable before money changes hands.
Before you start

items: The meeting, in a public place with a socket.
A phone with a torch.
A memory stick with a test file on it.
About thirty minutes.

body.text: Three tests in ten minutes

items: Ask to see it start from off, not from sleep.
Open the battery report, which shows the design capacity and the current one.
Type a sentence on a keyboard tester page, checking every letter.
Copy your test file across and open it, which tests the drive and the ports.
Play a video for two minutes with the sound on, which tests heat and speakers.
Ask to see the charger, since a missing one costs a real amount to replace.

body.text: You will see the battery report show a figure such as forty thousand against a design of fifty thousand, which means the battery has lost a fifth of its capacity. Anything below seventy per cent is a bargaining point.

body.alt: A command window showing a laptop battery report with design capacity and full charge capacity.
body.caption: Design capacity against full charge capacity. The difference is what the battery has lost, and it is written down.

body.text: It looks like a clean screen means a well-kept machine. Dust in the vents, a loose hinge, and a tired battery are invisible from the front, and all three are testable.
The parts that fail first

items: The hinge: open and close the lid slowly, and watch for a wobble or a crack.
The screen: look for bright spots or lines on a plain white page.
The keyboard: every key, including the ones you never use.
The trackpad: check the click and the edges where the cursor jumps.
The ports: plug something into each one, since a dead port is easy to hide.
The vents: shine a torch inside, and look for a mat of dust.

body.text: The keyboard test page will light up each key as you press it, which is the fastest way to find one that does not work. A single dead key is a reason to walk away on a laptop you cannot repair.

body.alt: A browser page showing a keyboard test with pressed keys highlighted.
body.caption: Press every key and watch the grid. A key that never lights up is a repair you will pay for later.

body.text: Questions for the seller

items: How long have you used it, and what did you use it for?
Has it ever been repaired, and by whom?
Is the drive the original one, or has it been replaced?
Is the charger the original, and does it charge at the normal speed?
Why are you selling it?
Will you let me run the battery report and the keyboard test?

body.text: None of this needs technical knowledge. A seller who answers easily and lets you test is the seller worth buying from.
Do not worry about asking to test. Anybody selling an honest machine expects it, and a refusal is the answer you needed.

body.alt: A hand opening a laptop lid slowly to check the hinge.
body.caption: Open the lid slowly and watch the hinge. A crack or a wobble becomes a broken screen within months.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here is a reason to negotiate, walk away, or plan a repair.

items: The seller will not let you test: walk away, since there is no reason to refuse.
The battery is below seventy per cent: price a replacement before agreeing.
The hinge is cracked: the screen will fail. Do not buy it at any price.
The charger is missing: add the cost to your offer, or ask them to include one.
It overheats within minutes: the vents are blocked, or the paste is gone.
You paid and found a fault: message at once, and keep the conversation in writing.

body.text: Practice
Test your own laptop, so you know what a good report looks like.

items: Open the battery report and note both capacity figures.
Type a sentence on a keyboard tester page.
Open and close the lid slowly, listening for a crack.
Shine a torch into the vents.
Write the three questions you would ask a seller.

body.text: You can now pay for a used machine with confidence. In the next lesson you will deal with chargers, cables, and the spark at the socket.
